title.value: Data Descriptor: GHWR, a multi- method global heatwave and warm-spell record and toolbox Background & Summary

scope_reason: The paper builds a global gridded heatwave/warm-spell record and uses it to characterise historical heatwave events (Chicago 1995, Europe 2003, Russia 2010).

scope_quote.evidence_text: In this paper, we introduce a multi-method global heatwave and warm-spell data record and analysis toolbox (named GHWR).

claims.restatement: Using a definition of daily maximum above 35°C for at least four days, the Midwest US and Chicago had around 5 heatwave days in July 1995, while South and Southwest US had many more.

relation_or_direction.value: around 5 heatwave days ... much more frequent in South and Southwest US

geography.value: Midwest US, and specifically Chicago; South and Southwest US

support_span.evidence_text: We analyze three historical heatwave events from around the globe that led to high societal impacts using the GHWR data set.

experimental_condition.value: heatwave defined as maximum daily temperatures above 35°C with a duration of at least four consecutive days

support_span.evidence_text: Figure 2a displays frequency of heatwave days defined based on the maximum daily temperatures above 35°C with a duration of at least four consecutive days.

evidence.evidence_text: While Midwest US, and specifically Chicago, experienced around 5 heatwave days in July of 1995 according to this definition, heatwave days were much more frequent in South and Southwest US.

claims.restatement: With heatwaves defined by minimum temperature above the local 90th percentile for at least four days, some western European locations had around 45 heatwave days in July-August 2003.

relation_or_direction.value: Some locations ... endure around 45 heatwave days in a two months period

support_span.evidence_text: We analyze three historical heatwave events from around the globe that led to high societal impacts using the GHWR data set.

experimental_condition.value: minimum daily temperature exceeding 90 th percentile of long-term distribution of TMIN ... for at least four consecutive days

evidence.evidence_text: Figure 3a displays the frequency of heatwave days over July and August, 2003 in western Europe, as defined by minimum daily temperature exceeding 90 th percentile of long-term distribution of TMIN for each day and each grid for at least four consecutive days. Some locations, interestingly, endure around 45 heatwave days in a two months period.

claims.restatement: With heatwaves defined by daily maximum above the local 90th percentile for at least four days, a large region around Moscow had 40+ heatwave days in July-August 2010.

experimental_condition.value: daily maximum temperature exceeding 90 th percentile of the long-term TMAX climatology for at least four consecutive days

support_span.evidence_text: Heatwave is defined by daily maximum temperature exceeding 90 th percentile of the long-term TMAX climatology for at least four consecutive days for each location and calendar day.

evidence.evidence_text: A large region surrounding Moscow, Russia, experienced 40+ heatwave days in two months.

claims.restatement: For Moscow in 2010, EHF and SHI responded differently in late July and mid September; the authors attribute this to EHF accounting for acclimation to recent weather while SHI does not.

concept.value: different response of these two metrics

support_span.evidence_text: Figure 5 displays daily time series of EHF (a) and SHI (b) values for Moscow, Russia, during June-September, 2010.
We analyze three historical heatwave events from around the globe that led to high societal impacts using the GHWR data set.
Figure 5 displays daily time series of EHF (a) and SHI (b) values for Moscow, Russia, during June-September, 2010.

evidence.evidence_text: The different response of these two metrics is rooted in their definitions, as EHF considers acclimation to recent weather conditions (mean daily temperature of the previous 30 days) whereas SHI does not include such an effect.
